\QLV{3} Given a natural number $n > 1$, show that the smallest divisor $d$ of $n$ such that $d > 1$ is prime using definition of prime numbers. We can assume all the basic properties of addition, multiplication and inequalities on the natural numbers. You may assume the well-ordering principle (Every non-empty set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of natural numbers has a least element, i.e. there exists a number $a \in A$, such that $a \leq x$, for all $x \in A$.)
\begin{proof}
output:
First, construct the set of non-trivial divisors of $n$. That is $D := \left\{ d \in \mathbb{N} | d>1, d|n\right\}$. By the well-ordering principle, there exists a least element of D, denote it $d'$. Suppose for contradiction that $d'$ is not prime, then it can be expressed that $d' = a \cdot b$ for $d'> a,b > 1$. However, it follows that both $a|n$ and $b|n$ so are elements of $D$ smaller than $d'$. This is a contradiction.
\end{proof}
feedback: Proof is correct, although it needs not be presented as a proof by contradiction. One could simply say that any $d' \mid d$ must either be equal to $d$ or $d' \not\in D$, so $d'=1$.

One can also use induction and we can assume all the basic properties of addition, multiplication and inequalities on the natural numbers.
\begin{proof}
output:
Define $S =\left\{  n\in\mathbb{N}|\exists a,b \in \mathbb{N}, n =a\cdot2 +b\cdot3 \right\}\cup \left\{ 0,1 \right\}$. Trivially 2 and 3 are in $S$. Next define $P = \mathbb{N}-S$, which by the well-ordering principle has a least element, $p$. As $0,1,2,3$ are in $S$, it follows that $p>3$ and so $0< p-3 < p$ and that $p-3$ must be in $S$ due to $p$ being the least element. However, this means that $(p-3)$ can be made from a combination of 2 and 3 cents and so adding another 3 cent to that combination yields $p$. This is a contradiction and so $P = \emptyset$ and $S = \mathbb{N}$. 
\end{proof}
feedback: Proof correct, complete, and well-presented. Construction of $S$ is a bit artificial, as it would be more natural to directly use well-ordering on numbers $\geq 2$ given the allowed tools.

Assuming only the well-ordering principle (Every non-empty set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of natural numbers has a least element, i.e. there exists a number $a \in A$, such that $a \leq x$, for all $x \in A$.) and strong induction principle. We can assume all the basic properties of addition, multiplication and inequalities on the natural numbers.
\begin{proof}
output:
By the well-ordering principle there exists a least element of $X$, call it $d$. By the second property of set $X$ we have that $d + d = 2d$ is in $X$, and by the same logic, if some $n \cdot d$ is in $X$ then $(n+1)\cdot d = nd + d$ is also in the set, so by induction, all multiples are in set. Now suppose for contradiction, there exists an element $g \in X$, such that $g$ is not a multiple of $d$. By the construction of $d$, it must be that $g > d$ so $g-d>0$ and by property 3 it follows that $g-d$ is in $X$. However, as $g > 0$, this new element is smaller than $d$ which is a contradiction.
